```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6, dpi = 96)
```

Logistic regression overestimates odds ratios in small samples: the maximum likelihood
coefficient is biased away from zero by about `b1 / n`. `logitbias` estimates `b1` the way
Nemes et al. did: draw many samples of each size from a population, fit a logistic regression to
each, and fit the mean coefficient against `1/n` by ordinary least squares. The intercept of that
fit is the large-sample value and the slope is `b1`. It also gives the analytic first-order bias
of the estimator for a population, and the bias-corrected estimate.

Nemes S, Jonasson JM, Genell A, Steineck G. Bias in odds ratios by logistic regression modelling
and sample size. *BMC Medical Research Methodology* 9:56 (2009).
[doi:10.1186/1471-2288-9-56](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-9-56)

## Install

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("jeonglab-bcm/fossil/PMC2724427/package")
```

```{r load}
library(logitbias)
packageVersion("logitbias")
```

## Example input

The bundled example holds a mean coefficient for each sample size from 100 to 1500 in steps of
5, for a continuous exposure `x` and a discrete exposure `z`, the shape of the paper's Fig. 1.
The means are synthetic: drawn around the curves of the paper's Table 1 (see
`example_path("README.md")`).

```{r input}
m <- read.csv(example_path("means_example.csv"))
dim(m)
head(m)
```

## Fit the bias curve

```{r fit}
fit <- fit_bias_curve(m)
fit[, c("term", "param", "estimate", "se", "t", "r2")]
```

```{r plot, fig.alt = "Mean coefficient against sample size, with the fitted curve beta + b1/n"}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (tm in c("x", "z")) {
  d <- m[m$term == tm, ]
  b <- fit$estimate[fit$term == tm]
  plot(d$n, d$mean, cex = 0.6, xlab = "Sample size", ylab = "Mean coefficient",
       main = if (tm == "x") "Continuous exposure" else "Discrete exposure")
  lines(d$n, b[1] + b[2] / d$n, lwd = 2)
}
par(op)
```

## Compare with the expected output

The expected output is the pair of values each curve was drawn from, with a tolerance of four
standard errors.

```{r compare}
e <- read.csv(example_path("means_example_expected.csv"))
cmp <- merge(fit[, c("term", "param", "estimate")], e, by = c("term", "param"))
cmp$within <- abs(cmp$estimate - cmp$value) <= cmp$tolerance
cmp
cat(sum(cmp$within), "of", nrow(cmp), "parameters match the expected output\n")
stopifnot(all(cmp$within))
```

## Run a small simulation

`simulate_population()` draws the paper's population of 100,000 (Additional file 1);
`bias_simulation()` draws samples of each size and fits each one. Samples in which a fitted
probability reaches 0 or 1 (separation, no finite estimate) are left out and counted. Here five
sizes and 200 samples per size keep it quick; the paper used 281 sizes and 1,000 samples.

```{r simulate}
pop <- simulate_population(100000, seed = 1)
sim <- bias_simulation(pop, sizes = c(100, 200, 400, 800, 1500), reps = 200, seed = 1)
sim$summary[, c("n", "term", "mean", "sd", "used", "dropped")]
fit_bias_curve(sim$summary)[, c("term", "param", "estimate", "se")]
```

The analytic first-order bias of the same population gives `b1` without any sampling:

```{r analytic}
round(analytic_bias(pop), 2)
```

A coefficient of 2.3 estimated from 150 people, with `b1 = 24`, corrects to:

```{r correct}
bias_correct(2.3, b1 = 24, n = 150)
```

## Your own data

- `fit_bias_curve(summary)` takes a data frame with columns `n` (sample size), `term`
  (coefficient name) and `mean` (mean estimate at that size). With `data = "all"` it also needs
  `used` (number of estimates) and `var` (their variance), and fits every estimate instead of the
  means.
- `bias_simulation(population, sizes, reps, seed)` takes a data frame with a 0/1 column `y` and
  numeric covariates. `drop` chooses which fits to leave out: `"boundary"` (any fitted
  probability within `1e-8` of 0 or 1), `"warning"` (only fits R warns about) or `"none"`.
  `cores` runs sizes in parallel; the result does not depend on it.
- Output columns of `fit_bias_curve()`: `estimate` is the large-sample coefficient
  (`intercept`) or `b1` (`inv_n`), with its standard error, t, p, the R squared of the fit and its
  degrees of freedom.
- `analytic_bias(population)` returns `b1` for each coefficient from the population's design;
  `bias_correct(estimate, b1, n)` subtracts `b1 / n`.

## The paper's full study

The reproduction runs the paper's whole design (281 sizes, 1,000 samples each, 20 populations)
and compares it with Table 1 and Figs 1 to 3: results page
<https://jeonglab-bcm.github.io/fossil/PMC2724427/>, pipeline
<https://github.com/jeonglab-bcm/fossil/tree/main/PMC2724427/figure-reproduction>.
